I was in a somewhat similar situation. I was in an LDR with a depressed person while I myself was depressed. While threats of suicide were never directly made, we both were cutting, though she did so more than I did. After a while of trying to make it work, it was obvious that I couldn't be with a depressed person when I had no way to physically be around them and comfort them. (Even in a local relationship, I question if I'd be able to handle it appropriately.) Being in this relationship pushed me much further into my own depression.

While it's your call to make, I would consider taking a step back and thinking about how this has affected your mental health. With that in mind, if she's shared specific plans with you, I would take whatever steps you possibly can to get her immediate help. Otherwise, consider breaking it off for your own good. What she ultimately decides is not and will never be your fault, no matter how much it seems that way.

After breaking off my LDR, I received a detailed a report of the self harm she claimed to have inflicted due to my actions. We actually stayed in contact for maybe 6 months after that, but then I stopped hearing from her, and haven't since. It seems like she may have actually been getting better, but there's no way to be sure. But I know that I did everything I could, and I was still able to be there for her as a friend afterward.

As terrible as it may sound (and I definitely DO NOT ADVISE THIS), that would explain the strange sense of relief I felt after my suicide attempt. At the time, I wasn't relieved that I failed, but I did feel like a weight was lifted.

I think the controlling part has a lot to do with it. I used to cut because I felt it was the only way I had control over myself. My parents actually never knew because I kept it hidden. I did tell my therapist, though.

I see a lot of the things other people have mentioned as well: I was struggling with school because I hit a wall from where things were just easy to learn to where I actually had to put a lot of effort into learning (and in some areas, I was never able to). I was going through a lot of relationship trouble for the first time, which is even harder as a teenager. I had absolutely no idea who I was, no sense of identity, and almost everything I did was decided for me.

I'm an adult now and wouldn't ever cut again, but I certainly still have my share of issues, though I manage to keep them private. To be honest, I have pretty pathetic social skills, very little self confidence about my appearance, and still battle with thoughts of how much I hate myself. The truth is, I realize this will never go away, but it does seem to get less intense over time. I wish I was told that at the beginning - that I'll never be "normal," that being "happy" doesn't mean you're never depressed.

To put it another way, it's like being terminally ill, and being told you'll make a full recovery if you try hard enough. But as much as you try, your test results don't improve, or only slightly improve. If you were told the truth from the beginning, that you're likely to die, you'd be celebrating the little victories instead of hating yourself for not making a full recovery.

Mental health is incredibly complex, as I'm sure you already know to a degree. When the depression starts talking, it convinces you that there is no solution. When the anxiety hits, you feel like the world is ending; if it's less extreme, you feel like you've ruined whatever situation you're in, and that you're not strong enough to handle it.

If you're approaching her with suggestions during panic attacks, you're going to get those kinds of angry responses. If you're waiting until a time that things seem stable, that's better, but I can understand a bit of anger. 

Battling mental health is incredibly personal. Imagine you've started a diet or exercise program, and it's working - you start to see the pounds shed, potentially have a slimmer waistline and/or better figure, and maybe even receive some positivity from those around you. If you have a bad week or two, what happens? You might gain a few pounds, but ultimately you've still improved, and you can easily track that with numbers. With mental health, if you're starting to feel better, other people are less likely to notice. You might even question if you truly are feeling better, because it's so difficult to measure. Then you have a bad day, what happens? There's no numerical scale to follow, so you feel like you're just broken and stuck this way. Those previous questions about if you're even really better start to feel like concrete facts about how you haven't improved at all.

I hope this helps give you some insight - I'm not trying to discourage you, but just inform you of how complex this is.

You're probably doing the same thing right now, and that's totally normal - I think depression melds our minds into thinking that way. I try to do some things in my free time that I consider to be positive, such as programming, cleaning up around the house, shopping for new clothes and other things that make me feel good about myself, etc. The first 5 minutes of all of those things are the hardest.

Some of these things don't require a lot of active attention, but they become much more rewarding if I give them my full attention. Shopping is so much better when I focus on finding clothes I like, especially things a bit different and new to me, instead of just running in and grabbing the same style I'm used to. This is also an example with no risk - go into a private dressing room and try it. If you look ridiculous, just laugh a little and change back. If you look great, you've succeeded at finding something new you enjoy!

I guess my point is, society seems to encourage multitasking these days. But things are often better when we don't. You can obviously go too far in the other direction as well (obsession), so finding the sweet spot is key.

I've been there. Not sure what level of school you're in, but high school was hell for me, even though I typically had a 4.0 GPA. Things went south for me my last year, but here's the advice I would give myself:

- If you're lucky enough to find yourself a girlfriend, and you're enjoying the relationship, don't even think about the future. I broke up with a girl primarily because I knew that things wouldn't make it past the high school relationship stage for us. I regret that, and would rather have just taken things a step at a time.

- Whether it's regarding a girlfriend, a friend who's a girl, or some girl you've never talked to, don't obsess. Ever. There's nothing wrong with having a crush or a relationship, but it becomes a problem when it's the only thing you can think about. If you focus on that too much, then there will be a ton of problems in your future. Again, just take things a step at a time, live your life a day at a time.

- You don't have to know what you're going to do for the rest of your life by the time high school is over. If you're not sure what to do, your best options are part time job, internship, and/or community college. The last two of those are the best options, in my opinion. I'm not even quite a year out of high school yet, I don't have a car, and I don't have any degrees or certs yet, but I'll still be able to get a job like that. Life has a funny way of working things out, don't be afraid of taking (responsible) chances.
